gaps.concept: The endometrial functionalis is shed during menstruation; the basalis remains and regenerates the lining.
gaps.why_tested: A histology or curettage stem asks which layer regenerates or why injury to the basalis causes amenorrhea.

gaps.concept: Estrogen drives the proliferative phase, producing straight tubular glands and mitotic stromal cells.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy taken before ovulation asks for the phase or dominant hormone.

gaps.concept: Progesterone drives the secretory phase, producing coiled, sawtooth glands with glycogen-rich secretions and stromal edema.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy after ovulation asks for the phase or hormone responsible.

gaps.concept: Corpus luteum regression causes progesterone withdrawal, spiral artery constriction, and shedding of the functionalis.
gaps.why_tested: A menstrual physiology stem asks what initiates bleeding in a cycle without pregnancy.

gaps.concept: Anovulation prevents corpus luteum formation, leaving estrogen unopposed by luteal progesterone and causing irregular endometrial bleeding.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with irregular cycles and bleeding has proliferative endometrium without secretory change.

gaps.concept: Endometriotic implants undergo cyclic hemorrhage; biopsy may show hemosiderin-laden macrophages, fibrosis, and adhesions.
gaps.why_tested: A pelvic lesion with old hemorrhage asks for the histologic clue or cause of pain.

gaps.concept: Endometriosis can impair fertility through pelvic adhesions and distortion of reproductive anatomy.
gaps.why_tested: An infertility stem asks how ectopic implants interfere with conception.

gaps.concept: Continuous GnRH agonist exposure downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, reducing LH, FSH, and ovarian estrogen after an initial flare.
gaps.why_tested: An endometriosis drug stem asks why continuous treatment suppresses estrogen despite an initial hormone rise.

gaps.concept: GnRH agonists and antagonists can cause hypoestrogenic hot flashes and bone loss during endometriosis treatment.
gaps.why_tested: A treated patient develops vasomotor symptoms or declining bone density.

gaps.concept: Danazol suppresses gonadotropins but causes androgenic adverse effects, including acne, hirsutism, and voice deepening.
gaps.why_tested: An endometriosis medication stem asks which drug explains new androgenic symptoms.

gaps.concept: Adenomyosis causes diffuse junctional-zone thickening and small myometrial cysts, unlike a sharply circumscribed leiomyoma.
gaps.why_tested: Uterine imaging asks which process explains an ill-defined, diffusely abnormal myometrium.

gaps.concept: Submucosal leiomyomas distort the endometrial cavity and are especially associated with heavy bleeding and infertility.
gaps.why_tested: An imaging stem asks which fibroid location best explains bleeding or impaired implantation.

gaps.concept: Leiomyomas usually shrink after menopause as ovarian steroid levels fall.
gaps.why_tested: A postmenopausal enlarging uterine mass asks why an ordinary fibroid is less likely.

gaps.concept: Leiomyosarcoma often presents as a solitary, rapidly enlarging, heterogeneous uterine mass after menopause.
gaps.why_tested: A mass vignette asks for a clue favoring sarcoma over multiple stable fibroids.

gaps.concept: Endometrial hyperplasia has crowded, irregular glands with an increased gland-to-stroma ratio but no stromal invasion.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy asks the histologic basis for hyperplasia or its distinction from carcinoma.

gaps.concept: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia, also called endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, is a precursor to endometrioid carcinoma.
gaps.why_tested: A pathology stem asks which premalignant lesion can progress to type I carcinoma.

gaps.concept: Endometrioid carcinoma forms atypical glands with stromal or myometrial invasion and commonly retains estrogen and progesterone receptors.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy asks how invasive type I carcinoma differs from atypical hyperplasia.

gaps.concept: Early menarche, late menopause, and nulliparity increase lifetime estrogen exposure and type I endometrial carcinoma risk.
gaps.why_tested: A risk-factor vignette asks which reproductive history increases endometrial cancer risk.

gaps.concept: Progestin exposure through pregnancy or combined oral contraceptives lowers endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma risk.
gaps.why_tested: A prevention or risk comparison asks why progesterone offsets estrogen-driven proliferation.

gaps.concept: Endometrial atrophy is a common benign cause of postmenopausal bleeding; cancer remains an important differential diagnosis.
gaps.why_tested: A postmenopausal bleeding stem asks for the likely cause or a key look-alike.

gaps.concept: Endometrial polyps contain irregular glands in fibrous stroma with thick-walled vessels and often cause intermenstrual spotting.
gaps.why_tested: A focal intracavitary lesion or biopsy asks for the diagnosis behind spotting.

gaps.concept: Asherman syndrome follows basalis injury, preventing endometrial regeneration and causing infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.
gaps.why_tested: A patient has scant menses and infertility after postpartum curettage.

gaps.concept: Postpartum endometritis presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and foul lochia; cesarean delivery increases risk.
gaps.why_tested: A febrile postpartum patient has a tender uterus and abnormal lochia.

gaps.concept: Acute endometritis shows neutrophils; chronic endometritis is distinguished by stromal plasma cells.
gaps.why_tested: An endometrial biopsy asks whether inflammation is acute or chronic.

gaps.concept: Uterine carcinosarcoma is usually a metaplastic epithelial malignancy with a shared clone across carcinomatous and sarcomatous components.
gaps.why_tested: A mixed uterine tumor stem asks for its cellular origin.

gaps.concept: The uterus develops from fused paramesonephric ducts; failed septum resorption yields a septate uterus with a normal external fundal contour.
gaps.why_tested: Recurrent pregnancy loss with two endometrial cavities and a smooth fundus asks for the embryologic defect.

gaps.concept: Failed paramesonephric duct fusion produces a bicornuate uterus with an externally indented fundus; complete failure produces uterus didelphys.
gaps.why_tested: Imaging asks whether a divided uterine cavity reflects failed fusion or failed septum resorption.
